description:
Operator: causal multi-head self-attention with ALiBi (Attention with Linear Biases) positional bias, as used in BLOOM-176B, MPT-7B/30B, BioGPT and Replit-code models. Instead of RoPE or learned position embeddings, each head h adds a fixed bias -m_h * (i - j) to the pre-softmax score for query position i and key position j <= i, where m_h = 2^(-8(h+1)/H) is a per-head geometric slope. Scores are computed from bf16 Q/K with f32 accumulation, scaled by 1/sqrt(D), the ALiBi bias and causal mask are applied in f32, softmax is taken in f32, probabilities are cast back to bf16 for the PV matmul (f32 accumulate), and the output is returned in the activation dtype.

Why it is not an exam operator: the exam's flash attention is plain causal MHA with only a boolean causal mask. ALiBi requires a per-head additive bias that depends on (head, query position, key position); a kernel cannot reuse a static mask tile and must synthesize the bias on-the-fly from the per-head slope and the tile's row/column indices inside the online-softmax loop, which changes the inner-loop fusion materially. It is also not GQA/MLA/paged/sparse/flex: it is dense, fully-materialized-position bias attention with H kv heads == H q heads.

Shapes (MPT-7B-like serving/training block): batch B=2, heads H=32, sequence S=2048, head_dim D=128, bf16 activations. Q, K, V each (2, 32, 2048, 128) bf16 = 32 MB, 96 MB total input; slopes is a (32,) f32 parameter. Output (2, 32, 2048, 128) bf16. The reference materializes the (2, 32, 2048, 2048) f32 score tensor (1 GB), which is acceptable for a baseline.

source_ref.spec: Multi-head attention with ALiBi positional bias (per-head slopes), causal, bf16, softmax in f32.

description:
Operator: causal sliding-window grouped-query attention with learned per-head attention-sink logits, as used in the gpt-oss sliding-window layers (and StreamingLLM-style sink attention). Each query head h has a scalar sink logit s_h that participates in the softmax normalizer (max and denominator) but contributes no value, so the probability mass over real keys sums to < 1; the mask is causal AND banded (key j visible to query i iff j <= i and i - j < window).

Why it is not an exam operator: it is not standard causal MHA, not plain GQA (the sink term changes the softmax normalization and the online-softmax recurrence a kernel must implement), not sparse/paged/MLA. The sink + banded-window fusion is the materially different part a Pallas kernel must handle (initialize the running max/denominator with the sink, skip key blocks outside the band).

Shapes (bf16 activations): q (4, 4096, 32, 128), k/v (4, 4096, 8, 128) -> 4:1 head ratio (Llama-3-8B style, not 8:1), head_dim 128, window 1024. Input bytes: q 128 MB + k 32 MB + v 32 MB = 192 MB. sinks (32,) float32 learned logits. Output (4, 4096, 32, 128) in input dtype.

Reference details: scores and softmax in float32 (dot_general preferred_element_type=f32), probabilities cast to the activation dtype for the PV matmul with f32 accumulation (matches kernel practice), normalization by (sum exp + exp(sink - m)). Computed in static query chunks of 512 that only touch the key range the band can reach, so peak f32 score memory stays ~400 MB instead of materializing a 4096x4096 score tensor. Deterministic: all inputs from jax.random.key(0) splits.

source_ref.spec: Grouped-query attention with attention sinks (learned per-head sink logits) and a sliding window; a head ratio other than 8:1.

description:
Operator: Gemma-3-style local (sliding-window) causal self-attention core. Each query at position q attends only to keys in (q - W, q], i.e. the last W=1024 tokens including itself, with the query pre-scaled by head_dim^-0.5. Gemma 2/3 interleave this local layer with global layers (5:1 in Gemma 3); the local layer is the one that dominates long-context decode/prefill cost and is what a Pallas kernel targets. Also uses Gemma 3's GQA head layout (16 query heads over 8 KV heads, head_dim 256).

Why not an exam operator: flash/GQA attention in the exam use a full causal mask over the whole sequence; here window << seq_len (1024 vs 8192) gives a banded mask, so the reference only materialises a 2W-wide key band per query block (K/V blocked with a zero-padded previous block, mask r < c <= W + r). A kernel must exploit the band (skip all blocks outside the diagonal and sub-diagonal) rather than reuse a causal flash loop, which is a materially different schedule and masking pattern.

Shapes/layout: fixed bf16 layout (B, S, H, D) for Q/K/V. B=1, S=8192, Hq=16, Hkv=8, D=256, W=1024. Input bytes: Q 64 MB + K 32 MB + V 32 MB = 128 MB. Logits, max, exp and normalisation all in float32 inside the reference; output cast back to the Q dtype. Deterministic inputs from jax.random.key(0).

source_ref.spec: Sliding-window causal attention (window << seq_len) with a fixed bf16 Q/K/V layout, softmax in f32.

description:
Operator: the paged KV-cache write step used by vLLM / JetStream-style serving engines (the `reshape_and_cache` / `write_to_kv_cache` op). After the attention projection of a decode-or-prefill step, each new token's K and V vectors (per KV head) must be scattered into a block-paged cache at the flat slot index given by `slot_mapping[token] = block_id * block_size + offset`. The cache uses the vLLM-TPU fused layout [num_blocks, block_size, 2*num_kv_heads, head_dim] (K heads then V heads along the head axis), stored in bf16. The op is a pure gather/scatter data-movement kernel: concatenate K/V along the head axis, view the cache as [num_blocks*block_size, 2*num_kv_heads, head_dim], scatter rows by slot, return the updated cache. No exam operator covers this: paged attention *reads* a paged cache, this is the *write* side (scatter by slot mapping), and it is not a reshape of any GEMM/attention/norm task.

Shapes (Llama-3-8B-like GQA: 8 KV heads × head_dim 128): num_blocks=4096, block_size=16 → 65,536 slots; kv_cache [4096,16,16,128] bf16 = 256 MB; num_tokens=8192 new tokens (a batched prefill chunk), new_k/new_v [8192,8,128] bf16 = 16 MB each; slot_mapping [8192] int32 drawn as a deterministic permutation of the slot space so indices are unique (making the scatter well-defined and deterministic). Total input ≈ 290 MB in bf16. Pure data movement, no accumulation needed; output cast to the cache dtype so bf16 is exact.

source_ref.spec: Write new K/V for a batch of sequences into a paged KV cache at given slot indices and return the updated cache (scatter by slot mapping, bf16).

description: Operator: weight-only int8 (W8A16) linear layer as used in quantized serving of Gemma-2 27B / Llama-style models (AQT / vLLM int8 weight-only path). The weight matrix W[N, K] is stored as int8 with a per-output-channel float32 scale s[N] (symmetric quantization, no zero point). The bf16 activations X[M, K] are multiplied by the dequantized weight: Y = (X @ W^T) * s, accumulated in float32, cast back to the activation dtype. A fused kernel would upcast int8 tiles to bf16 on the fly inside the MXU loop and apply the per-channel scale once per output tile in f32 rather than materializing a dequantized bf16 weight. This is not plain GEMM (mixed-dtype operands, fused dequant epilogue) and not any attention/MoE/norm exam operator. Shapes: Gemma-2 27B gate projection at prefill: M=2048 tokens, K=4608 hidden, N=36864 intermediate. Inputs: X bf16 2048x4608 (18.9 MB), W int8 36864x4608 (170 MB), scales f32 36864 (0.15 MB); output bf16 2048x36864 (151 MB).

source_ref.spec: Dequantize an int8 weight matrix with per-channel scales and multiply by bf16 activations, with f32 accumulation.

description: Operator: the MoE token router used in Qwen3-MoE / DeepSeek-V3-style decoders (norm_topk_prob=True variant). For every token: logits = x @ W_router (bf16 inputs, fp32 accumulate), softmax over experts in fp32, select the top-k experts, and renormalize the k selected probabilities to sum to 1. Returns (expert_indices int32 [T,k], expert_weights [T,k]). This is the router *scoring + selection* stage only — it is not the exam's sparse MoE dispatch (token gather/permute + expert FFN) nor Megablox grouped matmul; no expert weights or FFN are involved, and the fusion is GEMM -> softmax -> top-k -> renorm, which none of the exam ops cover. Shapes: T = 8 x 4096 = 32768 tokens, D = 4096 hidden, E = 128 experts, k = 8 (Qwen3-235B-A22B configuration). x is 32768x4096 bf16 = 256 MB, W_router is 4096x128 (1 MB). Top-k ties resolve to the lower expert index (lax.top_k semantics); logits std ≈ 1.28 so softmax is well-conditioned.

source_ref.spec: MoE router: logits = x @ W_router, softmax, top-k selection with renormalized weights, returning expert indices and weights (k=2 or 8, E=64..256 experts).

description:
Operator: per-head gated RMSNorm as used at the output of Gated DeltaNet (fla FusedRMSNormSwishGate, Qwen3-Next linear-attention blocks) and Mamba2's RMSNormGated with ngroups. The SSM/linear-attention output o (B, T, H, D) is RMS-normalized over the head dim D per head, scaled by a shared (D,) weight, then multiplied by silu(gate) where gate is the (B, T, H, D) output of the gate projection. Three fused elementwise/reduction stages (row reduce, scale, swish-gate multiply) with fp32 accumulation.

Why not an exam operator: plain RMSNorm is in the exam, but this is a materially different fusion — a second full-size activation tensor (the gate) is read, silu is computed and fused with the norm, and the reduction is over small per-head groups of 128 (H*D rows reshaped as grouped norm) rather than the full model dim. It is not attention, GEMM, MoE or SSD.

Shapes (bf16): x (4, 4096, 32, 128) = 128 MB, gate (4, 4096, 32, 128) = 128 MB, weight (128,). Total input ~256 MB; eps = 1e-6. Reference upcasts to float32, computes mean of squares per (b, t, h) row, rsqrt, scales by weight, multiplies by silu(gate), casts back to input dtype.

source_ref.spec: Gated RMSNorm as in Mamba2/Gated DeltaNet: normalize x, multiply by silu(gate), scale by weight.

description: Operator: the fused "add-then-norm" step of a pre-norm transformer block (vLLM's fused_add_rms_norm / TensorRT-LLM's residual-RMSNorm fusion). The incoming sub-layer output `x` (attention or MLP output) is added to the residual stream, the sum becomes the new residual stream (written back in bf16), and the same sum is RMS-normalised with f32 statistics using a Gemma-style (1 + scale) weight to produce the input of the next sub-layer. Both tensors are returned, so a Pallas kernel must read two bf16 streams once, accumulate the sum and sum-of-squares in f32 per row, and write two bf16 outputs — this is a different memory pattern and a dual-output contract versus the exam's single-input, single-output RMSNorm task (which has no residual add and no second output). Used in Gemma 3 / Llama 3 / Qwen decoder layers twice per block. Shapes: batch 4 x seq 4096 = 16384 tokens, hidden 5376 (Gemma 3 27B width), eps 1e-6; two bf16 activation inputs of 16384x5376 (~176 MB each, ~352 MB total) plus an f32 scale vector of 5376 (zeros, Gemma zero-centred init).

source_ref.spec: Pre-norm residual block fusion: residual add, then RMSNorm or LayerNorm, returning both the normed output and the updated residual stream (bf16 in, f32 statistics).

description: Operator: DeepSeek-V3 / DeepSeek-R1 style fine-grained blockwise FP8 GEMM. Both the activation matrix A (M, K) and the linear weight W (N, K) are stored as float8_e4m3fn with one float32 scale per 128x128 block (A scales: (M/128, K/128), W scales: (N/128, K/128)). The op computes Y = dequant(A) @ dequant(W)^T with f32 accumulation and a bf16 output, i.e. the fp8 linear used for every dense/expert projection in DeepSeek-V3 training and serving (the "fp8_gemm" with blockwise scales in the DeepSeek-V3 reference inference code). It is not an exam operator: plain GEMM has no quantization or scale tensors, and none of the attention/MoE/norm exam tasks involve fp8 block dequantization; a kernel must fuse per-K-block scale application into the accumulation loop, which is materially different from a plain matmul. Shapes (DeepSeek-V3 dense MLP up-projection at a 2048-token prefill chunk): M=2048, K=7168 (hidden), N=18432 (intermediate), block=128. Input footprint: A fp8 14.7 MB + W fp8 132 MB + scales ~1.1 MB ≈ 148 MB. create_inputs draws A ~ normal, W ~ normal*0.02 (from key(0) splits), then deterministically quantizes both to e4m3fn with per-128x128-block absmax/448 scales; the reference dequantizes in f32, runs lax.dot_general with preferred_element_type=f32, and casts to bfloat16.

source_ref.spec: Blockwise-scaled fp8 (float8_e4m3fn) matmul: inputs quantized in 128x128 blocks with f32 scales; dequantize-and-matmul in the reference.

description: Operator: fused QK-RMSNorm + rotary position embedding, as used in Qwen3 / Gemma 3 / OLMo-2 attention blocks. After the QKV projection, each Q head and each K head is independently RMS-normalised over head_dim with a learned per-dim scale (shared across heads), then rotate-half RoPE is applied using per-token positions. V is untouched and so excluded. This is not an exam operator: it is not attention itself, not a GEMM, and not a standalone RMSNorm — it is a two-op elementwise/row-reduction fusion over a 4-D GQA layout (Q and K have different head counts, D-dim reduction then pairwise rotation across the two halves of D) with f32 math and bf16 I/O. Shapes: batch 2, seq 8192, 32 Q heads, 8 KV heads, head_dim 128 → Q [2,8192,32,128] bf16 (134 MB) + K [2,8192,8,128] bf16 (34 MB) + positions [2,8192] int32 + two f32 [128] scales; eps 1e-6, rope_theta 1e6 (Qwen3). Reference computes norm, inv_freq, cos/sin and the rotation in float32 and casts back to the input dtype.

source_ref.spec: Apply QK-RMSNorm then rotary position embedding to Q and K for all heads (bf16 in, f32 math), returning rotated Q and K.

description: Semantics: torch.softmax(x, dim=1) on a 2-D (batch, features) input is a numerically-stable softmax along the last axis: subtract the per-row max, exp, divide by the per-row sum. Implemented explicitly in plain JAX (no Pallas) so the reference is unambiguous; inference mode, no parameters, no dropout/norm concerns. Shapes: KernelBench's default (4096, 393216) is ~6.4 GB f32, far above the 600 MB cap, so scaled down to batch=1024, dim=32768 → 1024*32768*4 B = 128 MB input (within 50–600 MB; 3x bytes = 384 MB, well under 20 GB). Both dimensions are multiples of 128 and batch is a multiple of 8. Input drawn from jax.random.uniform with key(0) to mirror torch.rand. Adapter converts the single torch input tensor to a jnp array (no transposes needed).

LogSoftmax over dim=1 of a 2D (batch, dim) tensor, inference-only, no parameters. Implemented explicitly in plain JAX as the numerically-stable form x - max - log(sum(exp(x - max))) along the last axis (matches torch.log_softmax(dim=1) for 2D input). KernelBench's default 4096x393216 is 6.4 GB f32, far over the 600 MB cap, so scaled to batch=1024, dim=32768 → 32M elements = 128 MB f32 input (both dims multiples of 128, batch >= 8). Input is uniform [0,1) like torch.rand, from jax.random.key(0).

Semantics: torch.nn.functional.gelu defaults to the exact erf-based GELU, so the port uses jax.nn.gelu(x, approximate=False) (JAX's default is the tanh approximation, which would not match). No parameters; single activation input from jax.random.uniform (matching torch.rand). Shapes: KernelBench's default 4096 x 393216 is 6.4 GB f32, far over budget, so scaled DOWN to batch=4096, dim=16384 (both multiples of 128) -> 256 MiB input, 3x = 768 MiB.

BatchNorm2d in training-style batch statistics (JAXBench convention): per-channel mean/biased variance over (N,H,W), eps=1e-5 (PyTorch default), gamma=ones, beta=zeros passed as explicit parameters. The previous port tripped the 5 GB RSS cap because KernelBench's default (64,64,512,512) is already 4.3 GB per copy. Scaled to (N=8, C=128, H=256, W=256) f32 = 268 MB of input (within the 50–600 MB window, channel/spatial dims multiples of 128, batch 8), so torch + JAX copies plus output stay well under the memory cap. Computation stays in NCHW (no transpose needed for a pure norm); variance uses the two-pass mean-of-squared-deviation form for numerical agreement with PyTorch.

The failure was a memory cap (6.3 GB > 5 GB), caused by the original 112x64x512x512 f32 input (7.5 GB). Shrunk to batch=16, features=64, 256x256 -> 16*64*256*256*4 = 268 MB input (within the 50-600 MB target; output same size, so torch+jax copies stay well under 5 GB). Semantics: nn.InstanceNorm2d default (affine=False, track_running_stats=False) -> normalize each (n, c) plane over H*W using biased variance, eps=1e-5, no scale/shift parameters. Only input is the activation x (NCHW). Mean/var computed in f32 via two-pass (mean, then mean of squared deviations) for numerical agreement with PyTorch.

GroupNorm over (N, C, H, W) with G groups, eps=1e-5 (PyTorch default), affine gamma=ones/beta=zeros passed as explicit inputs. Stats are computed per (sample, group) over C/G*H*W elements with biased variance, matching nn.GroupNorm. The previous port blew the 5 GB RSS cap (KernelBench's 112x64x512x512 input alone is 7.5 GB), so shapes are reduced: batch=8, features=128 (multiple of 128, divisible by 8 groups), dim1=dim2=256 -> input is 8*128*256*256*4 = 268 MB (within the 50-600 MB band, and ~10 copies stay well under 5 GB). The workload is written to avoid extra full-size temporaries beyond the centered tensor (reshape to (N,G,-1), mean/var via two reductions, single normalize/affine expression). The adapter converts the torch input to numpy without copies and reads gamma/beta from the torch GroupNorm parameters.

Op: L2 normalization along dim=1, y = x / ||x||_2 (keepdim). No parameters, no eps (PyTorch torch.norm has none, so none is added). Only input is the activation x. Implementation uses sum of squares along axis 1 + sqrt, matching torch.norm(p=2). KernelBench default (32768 x 65535 f32 = 8.6 GB) is far above the budget, so scaled to batch=2048, dim=16384 (both multiples of 128): 33.5M elements = 134 MB f32, within the 50-600 MB window. Inputs from jax.random.uniform(key(0)) to mirror torch.rand.

LayerNorm over the trailing (features, dim1, dim2) axes with eps=1e-5 (PyTorch default), elementwise affine with gamma=ones, beta=zeros passed as explicit parameters of shape (features, dim1, dim2). Computed in f32 with mean and biased variance over the normalized axes. Shapes kept at KernelBench defaults (batch=16, features=64, dim1=dim2=256) since the input is already 16*64*256*256*4 B = 268 MB, in the 50-600 MB window; all dims are multiples of 8/128 as applicable.

Single nn.Conv2d(3->96, k=11, stride=4, padding=2, bias=True), inference. Interface keeps PyTorch NCHW input; inside, transpose to NHWC, run lax.conv_general_dilated with explicit padding ((2,2),(2,2)) and stride 4, add bias, transpose back to NCHW. Weight passed in HWIO layout (11,11,3,96) with bias (96,). Shapes: KernelBench default (256,3,224,224) f32 is already ~154 MB, in the 50-600 MB window, so kept as-is (channels=3 can't be a multiple of 128 for this op; batch 256 is a multiple of 8). Output (256,96,55,55). Weights init normal*0.02, bias normal*0.02.

Semantics: nn.Conv3d with kernel 3, stride 1, padding 0 ('VALID'), dilation 1, groups 1, bias=False — a single lax.conv_general_dilated. Interface keeps PyTorch layouts: activation NCDHW, weight OIDHW (out, in, kD, kH, kW). Inside workload: transpose x to NDHWC and w to DHWIO, run conv with dimension_numbers ('NDHWC','DHWIO','NDHWC'), transpose result back to NCDHW. Weight initialised as normal*0.02; activation uniform from key(0). Shapes scaled: batch 16, in_channels 3->8, out_channels 64, D=H=W=64 -> input 16*8*64^3*4 B = 134 MB (within 50-600 MB), weight tiny, output (16,64,62,62,62) f32 ~976 MB; 3x input well under 20 GB. All sizes in CONFIG; workload reads channel/kernel sizes from array shapes.

MSE loss: mean((pred - target)^2), reduced in f32 to a scalar. The previous failure was a torch.rand signature error raised inside the adapter (it tried to rebuild/scale inputs with torch.rand). The new adapter does no torch RNG at all: it just takes the two tensors from get_inputs() (predictions already carry the random scale) and converts them to numpy -> jnp in order. Shapes scaled from KernelBench's 32768x32768 (4 GB each) down to batch=4096, dim=8192 per array (128 MB each, 256 MB total f32 input, multiples of 128). create_inputs draws predictions as uniform * a deterministic scalar scale (uniform from a split key) and targets as uniform, mirroring get_inputs. workload reads nothing from literals; shapes come from the arrays.

Op chain: x @ W^T + b (nn.Linear, weight passed as (in, out)), GroupNorm over (batch, out_features) with num_groups=16 groups of 512 channels each, per-sample/per-group mean & biased variance, eps=1e-5 (PyTorch default), affine gamma=ones/beta=zeros, then Hardtanh clip to [-2, 2]. Shapes: KernelBench defaults already land in range — x (1024, 8192) f32 = 32 MB, W (8192, 8192) = 256 MB, bias/gamma/beta 8192 each; total ≈ 288 MB, all dims multiples of 128, batch 1024. Inputs: x uniform [0,1) like torch.rand, W normal*0.02, bias normal*0.02, GN scale=ones, shift=zeros. Everything deterministic from jax.random.key(0).

Semantics: y = x @ W^T + b (nn.Linear, so weight passed as (in, out) and used as x @ w), then y * scale (per-output-feature vector, mirrors torch.randn(scale_shape) so sampled as plain unit normal rather than *0.02 — it is a multiplicative param, not a GEMM weight, and unit scale keeps the BN variance well above eps), then BatchNorm1d with BATCH statistics (JAXBench convention): biased variance over the batch axis, eps=1e-5, gamma=ones, beta=zeros passed as explicit inputs. Dropout/momentum irrelevant in inference. Shapes: KernelBench defaults already land in range — batch=1024, in=8192, out=8192 (all multiples of 128): x = 32 MB, W = 256 MB, total ≈ 288 MB f32 (3x ≈ 0.86 GB). Output f32 (1024, 8192). Input order: x, w (in,out), b, scale, gamma, beta.

Op chain: Linear (x @ w + b) -> elementwise scale by per-feature vector -> BatchNorm1d using batch statistics (biased variance, eps=1e-5) with explicit gamma=ones/beta=zeros inputs. Shapes kept at KernelBench defaults since they already satisfy the budget: batch=16384, in=4096, out=4096 (x = 256 MB, w = 64 MB, total ~320 MB, all multiples of 128). nn.Linear weight passed as (in, out); w and b ~ normal*0.02; scale ~ unit normal mirroring torch.randn(scale_shape) so pre-BN variance is not eps-dominated; gamma/beta deterministic ones/zeros. Inference semantics (no running-stat update), fully deterministic from jax.random.key(0).

Semantics: nn.Linear as x @ w + b with w passed as (in, out) (PyTorch stores (out, in); adapter transposes). GroupNorm on a 2D (N, C) activation: reshape to (N, G, C/G), normalize over the last axis with biased variance and eps=1e-5, then per-channel affine with gamma=ones, beta=zeros (module default, inference). LeakyReLU slope 0.01 via jnp.where, then x + x. Shapes: KernelBench defaults already land in range — x (1024, 8192) = 32 MB, w (8192, 8192) = 256 MB, bias/gamma/beta 32 KB each, ~288 MB total (<600 MB, 3x < 20 GB), all dims multiples of 128, batch 1024 multiple of 8. So I kept batch=1024, input=8192, hidden=8192, groups=512 (16 channels per group). Deterministic inputs from jax.random.key(0); weights normal*0.02; norm params constants.

Op chain: Linear (x @ W^T + b) -> ReLU -> divide by constant. Inference mode, no dropout/BN. nn.Linear weight (out,in) is passed to workload transposed as (in,out) so workload does x @ w + b. Divisor lives in CONFIG. Shapes: KernelBench defaults already in range (batch=1024, in=8192, out=8192): x = 32 MB, w = 256 MB, b = 32 KB, total ~288 MB f32, all dims multiples of 128; kept as-is. x from jax.random.uniform (matches torch.rand), weights normal*0.02, bias normal*0.02.

Semantics: nn.Linear as x @ w + b with w passed as (in, out). logsumexp over dim=1 with keepdim (output shape (B,1)); two leaky_relu with slope 0.01 (jax.nn.leaky_relu, negative_slope=0.01); two exact erf-based GELU (jax.nn.gelu with approximate=False to match PyTorch default). Inference mode, no dropout/norm. Shapes: KernelBench defaults already in range — batch 1024, in 8192, out 8192 → x 32 MB + w 256 MB + b ≈ 288 MB of f32 input, all dims multiples of 128. Weight init normal*0.02, bias normal*0.02, activations uniform like torch.rand.

Op chain: Linear (x @ W^T + b) -> swish (x*sigmoid(x)) -> divide by 2 -> clamp[-1,1] -> tanh -> clamp[-1,1]. Inference mode, no stochastic ops. nn.Linear weight is passed to workload pre-transposed as (in, out) so the kernel is `x @ w + b`. The second clamp is kept for fidelity even though tanh output is already in [-1,1]. Shapes: KernelBench defaults batch=1024, in=8192, out=8192 already give x=32 MB + w=256 MB + b=32 KB ≈ 288 MB of f32 input (within 50–600 MB), all dims multiples of 128, batch multiple of 8, so they are kept as-is. Activations from jax.random.uniform (matching torch.rand), weight normal*0.02, bias normal*0.02. Divisor and clamp bounds live in CONFIG.

Semantics: nn.Linear as x @ w with w passed (in, out) plus bias b; extra bias add; Hardtanh = clip to [-1, 1]; Mish = x * tanh(softplus(x)) (numerically safe softplus via jax.nn.softplus); GroupNorm over 2D (N, C) input: reshape to (N, G, C/G), normalize with biased variance and PyTorch default eps=1e-5, then affine with gamma=ones, beta=zeros (GroupNorm default init). Inference mode, no dropout/BN involved. Shapes: KernelBench defaults already in range — batch 1024, in_features 8192, out_features 8192, num_groups 256 (32 channels/group). Input bytes: x 32 MB + weight 256 MB + small vectors ≈ 288 MB (f32), all dims multiples of 128. Weights/biases drawn as normal * 0.02, activations uniform from key(0).

Target the GQA decode path (ragged_gqa -> vmap over ragged_mqa -> ragged_flash_attention_kernel). Config: B=8, Hq=32, Hkv=8, D=128, S=2048, block_size=256, bf16 activations, int32 ragged lengths. Reference computes the same contract as ragged_gqa: unnormalized output o*l (sum of exp(logit - max) @ v in f32), running max m, and denominator l, all with the DEFAULT_MASK_VALUE additive mask. Kernel module inlines the flash kernel, ragged_mqa's pallas_call with the PrefetchScalarGridSpec and ragged block-index prefetch, and the ragged_gqa wrapper; cost_estimate/interpret knobs removed.

description: Target one realistic configuration of the blockwise (sub-channel) quantized matmul: bf16 activations [1024, 4096], int8 weights [4096, 4096] with block_size=128 along the input dim, f32 weight scales [32, 1, 4096], and int8 activation quantization (x_q_dtype=int8) done per 128-wide block inside the kernel. Tuned block sizes fixed to batch_block=512, out_block=1024, in_block=1024, n_lane_multiplier=1 (steps_k=8, steps_n=4). Inline util.quantize_block (symmetric absmax per-row quantization) and unfold_args (nested lax.cond unrolling of the first/last-step flags); drop padding / tuning table / zero-point / channelwise knobs. The kernel's int32 accumulator override is dead in this source (acc_scratch is bf16, so storing an int32 block would fail abstract eval), so the accumulator is the bf16 path the kernel actually runs. Reference mirrors the exact op order in plain JAX: per-block f32 absmax -> int8 quantize, int8xint8 dot with int32 result, cast to bf16, multiply by activation scale (bf16) then weight scale (bf16), sequential bf16 accumulation over the 32 blocks, cast to x.dtype.

Pick one realistic configuration of structured_spmm: activation (M,K) @ sparse_weight.T where the weight is stored (N,K) (PyTorch Linear layout), 2:4 sparse along the contracting dim K with stride=128 -> rhs_sparse=True, contract_sparse=True, rhs_transpose=True -> sparse_dim=1. Shapes M=256, K=4096, N=4096, blocks (256, 512, 512), grid (1, 8, 8). Metadata is 2-bit indices packed 16 per int32 row. Inputs to workload are (nonzeros, metadata, activation): create_inputs generates random nonzeros/activation and random distinct in-group indices, then packs them exactly like Sparsifier.compress. The reference unpacks metadata, rebuilds the dense f32 (N,K) weight with the same where-chain / strided-group layout as _decompress_nonzeros, and does an f32 HIGHEST-precision transposed-RHS matmul, casting to the inferred out dtype. The kernel module inlines _decompress_metadata, _decompress_nonzeros (sparse_dim=1 path), _infer_out_dtype and the pallas_call with the BlockSpecs specialized to this (rhs_sparse, rhs_transpose, sparse_dim=1) mapping; math unchanged.
